sections.title: Bios, Uefi, And Post
sections.content:
FIRMWARE FUNDAMENTALS.
Firmware is low-level code stored in flash memory on the motherboard. It runs before any operating system. Firmware responsibilities: initializing all hardware components, performing POST â€” the Power-On Self-Test â€” and locating and handing off execution to the bootloader on the primary storage device.
BIOS vs UEFI.
BIOS â€” Basic Input/Output System â€” is the legacy firmware standard.
Text-based configuration interface, navigated with keyboard only.
Supports MBR â€” Master Boot Record â€” partitioning, with a maximum disk size of 2.2 TB.
Operates in 16-bit and 32-bit processor modes.
Slower boot process.
Minimal security features â€” no Secure Boot support.
UEFI â€” Unified Extensible Firmware Interface â€” is the modern replacement.
Graphical interface supporting mouse navigation.
Supports GPT â€” GUID Partition Table â€” partitioning with no disk size limit.
Operates in 64-bit mode.
Faster boot process.
Secure Boot support.
TPM integration.
Network access during pre-boot.
Can operate in CSM mode â€” Compatibility Support Module â€” to emulate legacy BIOS for older operating systems.
ACCESSING FIRMWARE.
During POST, press the appropriate key to enter the firmware settings. Common keys: Delete, F2, F10, F12, Escape. The specific key depends on the motherboard manufacturer. If the window is missed, access firmware from Windows through: Settings â†’ Update & Security â†’ Recovery â†’ Advanced startup â†’ UEFI firmware settings.
POST â€” POWER-ON SELF-TEST.
POST runs at every startup. It verifies that essential hardware â€” CPU, RAM, video, and storage â€” is present and functional. POST takes place before the operating system loads.
If POST detects a problem before the video system is initialized â€” meaning the display is not yet functional â€” the motherboard communicates through beep codes: audio tones generated by the system speaker. The number and pattern of beeps map to specific hardware failures. Beep code meanings vary by manufacturer â€” consult the motherboard documentation. Common patterns on AMI BIOS: one long beep followed by multiple short beeps often indicates RAM failure.
BOOT ORDER AND BOOT FAILURES.
Boot order in UEFI determines which device is searched first for a bootable OS. If the configured boot device is missing, the firmware produces errors such as "Boot device not found" or "No bootable device."
Common boot failure causes: drive not detected â€” check data and power cables, check UEFI storage detection. Incorrect boot order â€” USB drive or optical media is set as first boot device. Secure Boot mismatch â€” unsigned bootloader prevented from executing. SATA mode mismatch â€” AHCI vs RAID setting does not match the existing drive configuration.
MBR vs GPT.
MBR is the legacy partition scheme: supports a maximum of four primary partitions, and the 2.2 TB disk size limit. Works with BIOS and UEFI in legacy mode.
GPT is the modern partition scheme: supports up to 128 primary partitions on Windows, no disk size limit, stores redundant copies of partition data, and is required for UEFI Secure Boot.
SECURE BOOT AND TPM.
Secure Boot is a UEFI feature that validates the bootloader and OS kernel using cryptographic signatures before executing them. Secure Boot prevents boot-level malware â€” rootkits that load before the OS â€” from establishing themselves. Installing a Linux distribution with an unsigned bootloader may require disabling Secure Boot temporarily.
TPM â€” Trusted Platform Module â€” is a hardware chip that securely stores cryptographic keys, certificates, and hashed credentials. TPM provides the hardware root of trust that Secure Boot depends on for key validation. TPM is also used by BitLocker full-disk encryption to store the encryption key tied to the specific hardware configuration.
HSM â€” Hardware Security Module â€” is an external device, typically USB, that provides secure key storage when a TPM is not available or when the encrypted drive needs to be moved to a different system.
BIOS/UEFI SECURITY SETTINGS.
Beyond Secure Boot and TPM, firmware provides additional access controls that the exam tests explicitly.
Supervisor password â€” also called BIOS password or Setup password: a password required to access and modify BIOS/UEFI settings. Without the supervisor password, a user can power on and boot the system normally, but cannot change any firmware configuration â€” boot order, Secure Boot settings, virtualization support, or any other BIOS option. This is the administrative password for the firmware interface itself. Critical in environments where BIOS hardening is required to prevent users from reconfiguring boot order to boot from USB or disabling Secure Boot.
Boot password â€” also called Power-On password or Pre-Boot Authentication password: a password required before the system will begin the boot process at all. The prompt appears before POST completes and before the OS loads. This is a stronger access control than the supervisor password â€” it stops anyone from using the system entirely, not just from changing settings. Boot password loss typically requires physically clearing the CMOS via the dedicated jumper on the motherboard, which resets all BIOS settings to factory defaults. Some enterprise systems require a vendor service key to recover.
USB port security in BIOS/UEFI: the firmware can disable USB functionality at the hardware level before the OS loads.
Disabling USB booting: prevents booting from a USB drive even if the user can access the BIOS boot menu. Blocks unauthorized OS images, live-boot tools, and bootable diagnostic media from being executed.
Disabling all USB ports: prevents data exfiltration via USB storage devices and blocks unauthorized device connections entirely â€” enforced at the firmware level, not dependent on OS policies or group policy, and not bypassable even by an OS-level administrator.
These controls are set in BIOS/UEFI settings and are the first line of physical security hardening on a workstation or server.
CMOS BATTERY.
The CMOS battery â€” a CR2032 coin cell on the motherboard â€” maintains the real-time clock and BIOS/UEFI settings when the system is powered off. When the CMOS battery fails, the system clock resets to a default date â€” often January 1, 2000 or January 1, 2001 â€” and all BIOS settings return to factory defaults at every power cycle. The fix is straightforward: identify the CR2032 on the motherboard and replace it.
---
exam_tips: MBR = BIOS, 2.2 TB limit. GPT = UEFI, no size limit, required for Secure Boot. These are the two key structural differences.

sections.title: Power Supply Troubleshooting
sections.content:
PSU FUNCTION.
The power supply unit converts AC from the wall to the DC voltages the system uses: 12V for fans, motors, and high-power components; 5V and 3.3V for logic circuits and storage. When the PSU achieves stable output voltages, it sends a Power Good signal to the motherboard. The CPU does not begin operating until Power Good is received. If Power Good is never sent â€” because the PSU cannot stabilize its output â€” the system will not POST.
PSU TROUBLESHOOTING SEQUENCE.
Step 1: Test the wall outlet with a known-good device. Confirm power is present.
Step 2: Check the PSU's power switch on the rear panel â€” ensure it is in the on position.
Step 3: Inspect the power cord for damage and try a known-good replacement.
Step 4: Remove non-essential peripherals â€” graphics cards, extra drives, expansion cards. An undersized PSU may fail to start under its full load.
Step 5: Use a PSU tester to verify output voltages, or test with a multimeter.
Step 6: Substitute a known-good PSU if available.
WARNING: Do not open a PSU. Internal capacitors retain lethal voltage levels even after the unit has been unplugged for extended periods. PSUs are sealed, non-serviceable components â€” replace, do not repair.
---
exam_tips: If the system beeps but shows no video, POST failed before the display was initialized. Count and pattern the beeps, then consult the motherboard manufacturer's beep code reference.

sections.title: Storage Failure
sections.content:
FAILURE SYMPTOMS.
Clicking or grinding sound from an HDD: the read head is failing to locate or read sectors. This is a mechanical failure in progress. Back up all data immediately â€” the drive should be considered failed. Every additional click is additional risk of total data loss.
No drive activity LED: either no power is reaching the drive, or the drive has completely failed. Check power and data connections first.
Constant disk activity with no apparent tasks: disk thrashing â€” the system is paging excessively to disk because RAM is insufficient. Identify by checking RAM utilization. Address by adding RAM, not replacing the drive.
Read/write errors, file system corruption, BSODs with disk-related stop codes, or files that appear corrupted: bad sectors â€” physical regions of the drive that can no longer reliably store data.
Drive not detected: check SATA or NVMe data and power connections. Verify UEFI detects the drive. Check for SATA mode mismatch.
SMART â€” SELF-MONITORING, ANALYSIS, AND REPORTING TECHNOLOGY.
SMART is embedded in all modern HDDs and SSDs. It continuously monitors internal health metrics: error rates, reallocated sector counts, spin-up time, write errors, and drive temperature. Reallocated sectors â€” areas of the drive remapped from bad to spare sectors â€” are a critical indicator. Increasing counts mean the drive is running out of spare sectors and failure is approaching.
Use SMART utilities â€” CrystalDiskInfo on Windows, or manufacturer-provided tools â€” to check drive health regularly, especially on drives showing symptoms.
SSD note: SSD data recovery after failure is typically difficult or impossible. Unlike HDDs, where data sometimes persists after head failure, SSD failure often makes data irrecoverable due to the controller's wear-leveling behavior.
RAID FAILURE.
Degraded array: one drive has failed in a RAID 1, 5, 6, or 10 configuration. The array is still accessible â€” data integrity is maintained. Replace the failed drive immediately. During the rebuild process the array is vulnerable â€” a second drive failure at this point may cause complete array loss.
Hot-swap: identify the failed drive correctly before removing it. Remove the wrong drive during a rebuild and the array fails instantly. Check the RAID controller's management interface to confirm which drive slot contains the failed disk before touching anything.
RAID 0 has no redundancy â€” any single drive failure results in total data loss across the stripe.
Reminder: RAID is not a backup. RAID provides redundancy against hardware failure â€” it does not protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, or corruption that propagates to all mirrors simultaneously.
---
exam_tips: Power Good signal from PSU triggers POST. If PSU cannot stabilize output, Power Good is not sent and the system will not start â€” fans may spin briefly but nothing else happens.

sections.title: System Stability
sections.content:
OVERHEATING.
Overheating is one of the most common causes of system instability. Symptoms: random shutdowns â€” the CPU or motherboard triggers a thermal emergency shutdown to prevent damage. Thermal throttling â€” the CPU reduces its clock speed to lower heat generation, resulting in noticeably reduced performance under load. Crashes specifically under load but not at idle. In severe cases, a burning smell.
Diagnostic checklist: verify the CPU fan is spinning. Check that the heatsink is properly mounted with full contact area â€” a heatsink installed without proper thermal paste, or improperly seated, will not transfer heat. Inspect the thermal paste â€” old dried paste has poor conductivity and should be replaced. Verify case airflow â€” intake and exhaust fans must be functioning. Check the environment â€” a system in a hot room or enclosed cabinet runs hotter than one in an air-conditioned environment.
RAM FAILURES.
RAM issues produce random crashes, BSODs, application errors, and POST failures. A system that will not POST may show a RAM-related beep code. A system that posts but crashes randomly, especially under memory-intensive workloads, suspects RAM.
Diagnosis: remove and reseat all RAM modules â€” dirty contacts cause intermittent failures. Test one module at a time to identify which one is failing. Run memory diagnostic software: Windows Memory Diagnostic (built-in) or MemTest86 (bootable, more thorough). Verify the installed RAM specifications are on the motherboard's QVL â€” Qualified Vendor List.
BSOD â€” BLUE SCREEN OF DEATH.
Windows BSODs include a stop code â€” a hexadecimal value or text description identifying the type of failure. Note the stop code. Common causes: faulty or incompatible device drivers (the most common BSOD cause), corrupt system files, hardware failures â€” RAM, storage, GPU â€” and overheating.
Physical damage inspection: before assuming software or configuration causes, inspect hardware. Look for: bent CPU socket pins, broken port bodies, liquid damage residue and corrosion, scorch marks on the PCB, bulging capacitors on the motherboard, and cracked PCB traces. ESD damage and power surges may not be immediately visible but cause intermittent or permanent failures.
PERFORMANCE TROUBLESHOOTING.
When performance degrades suddenly: first question is always "What changed?" Recent hardware additions, driver updates, software installs, and configuration changes are the most common cause of sudden performance regression. Identify the change and reverse it if possible.
---
exam_tips: An HDD making clicking or grinding noises is in mechanical failure. Back up data immediately â€” do not continue using the drive. Every additional access risks total data loss.
Bulging capacitors on the motherboard are a sign of electrical failure. They cause intermittent or total system instability and require motherboard replacement.

concept_cards.hook: POST is not just a startup animation â€” it is the system verifying that the hardware required to run an operating system is actually present and functional. When it fails, the beep codes tell you which component to look at.
concept_cards.summary: Firmware is the low-level code stored in flash memory on the motherboard. It runs before the operating system loads, initializes hardware, performs POST â€” the Power-On Self-Test â€” and locates and hands off to the bootloader.

concept_cards.hook: An HDD that makes a clicking noise is not a minor issue â€” it is a drive about to fail. Every click is the read head attempting and failing to find a sector. Back up the data immediately and replace the drive.
concept_cards.summary: PSU troubleshooting sequence: start at the wall. Test the outlet with a known-good device.

concept_cards.hook: A system that crashes at full load but runs fine at idle is not a mystery â€” it is an overheating problem. The CPU is throttling and then halting as it exceeds its thermal limit. The solution is in the cooling system, not the software.
concept_cards.summary: Overheating symptoms: random shutdowns under load, thermal throttling â€” reduced performance as the CPU slows itself to reduce heat generation â€” crashes during CPU-intensive tasks, and in severe cases a burning smell. Diagnose with temperature monitoring software.

PSU FUNCTION. The power supply unit converts AC from the wall to the DC voltages the system uses: 12V for fans, motors, and high-power components; 5V and 3.3V for logic circuits and storage. When the PSU achieves stable output voltages, it sends a Power Good signal to the motherboard.
FAILURE SYMPTOMS. Clicking or grinding sound from an HDD: the read head is failing to locate or read sectors. This is a mechanical failure in progress.

practice_questions.q: A PC powers on with fans spinning but no POST and no display output. What component should be reseated FIRST?
options: GPU
CPU
RAM
Hard drive

practice_questions.q: A PC emits three short beeps during POST (AMI BIOS) and fails to boot. What does this indicate?
options: Successful POST completion
Power supply failure
CPU failure
RAM error â€” memory not detected or failed
practice_questions.explanation: On AMI BIOS, three short beeps indicate a RAM/memory error (no memory installed, or memory failure). Note: beep codes are vendor-specific. On AMI BIOS, one short beep = successful POST. Always identify the BIOS manufacturer before diagnosing by beep pattern.

practice_questions.q: What tool measures voltages from a PSU to verify it is providing correct power levels?
options: Multimeter or dedicated PSU tester
POST card
Cable continuity tester
Logic analyzer

practice_questions.q: A computer randomly shuts off only under heavy load. Airflow is clear and all fans work. The MOST likely cause is:
options: Bad RAM
Bad monitor connection
Inadequate or failing power supply unable to sustain load
Corrupt operating system

practice_questions.q: A PC displays "CPU fan error" at startup but the fan is visibly spinning. What else could trigger this message?
options: Fan speed below the BIOS minimum threshold, or the fan connected to the wrong header
CPU temperature too high
CPU requires replacement
Thermal paste is missing

practice_questions.q: Which CPU socket type features pins on the motherboard socket and a flat contact pad on the CPU (used by Intel)?
options: LGA (Land Grid Array)
AM4 (PGA)
FM2 (AMD)
TR4

practice_questions.q: A hard drive produces a clicking noise during operation. What does this indicate?
options: Normal operation when accessing files
Drive spinning up normally after a cold start
Mechanical failure â€” the read/write head is failing, data is at risk â€” back up immediately
Vibration from a nearby case fan

practice_questions.q: A RAID 5 array loses one drive and is now in a degraded state. What should the technician do?
options: Immediately shut down and restore from backup
Replace the failed drive as soon as possible to allow the array to rebuild
Delete the RAID configuration and start over
Continue using it as-is since data is still accessible

practice_questions.q: What does a S.M.A.R.T. status of "Caution" or "Failing" indicate?
options: Drive is operating normally with minor warnings
Drive has detected internal errors and potential imminent failure â€” back up data immediately
Drive needs defragmentation
Drive firmware needs updating

practice_questions.q: A system clock resets to January 1, 2001 every time the computer is powered off and back on, and BIOS settings are lost between boots. What is the most likely cause?
options: The operating system is corrupt
The CMOS battery has failed and needs replacement
The hard drive has failed
The CPU is overheating
practice_questions.explanation: The CMOS battery — a CR2032 coin cell on the motherboard — maintains the real-time clock and BIOS/UEFI settings when the system is powered off. When it fails, the clock resets to a factory default date and all BIOS settings revert to defaults on every power cycle. Replacing the CR2032 resolves this.

practice_questions.q: A technician wants to prevent any user from booting the computer from a USB drive or changing the boot order, even if they can access the BIOS menu. Which BIOS security setting accomplishes this?
options: Boot password (power-on password)
Supervisor password (setup password)
Secure Boot
TPM configuration
practice_questions.explanation: The supervisor password (also called the BIOS or setup password) prevents access to and modification of BIOS/UEFI settings. Without it, the user cannot change the boot order or enable USB booting. The boot password prevents the system from booting at all — it does not protect settings from the boot menu.

practice_questions.q: A system experiences random crashes and BSODs only when running memory-intensive applications, but runs fine at idle. Which diagnostic tool should be used to test RAM?
options: CrystalDiskInfo
Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86
Device Manager
SMART utility
practice_questions.explanation: Random crashes and BSODs under memory-intensive workloads are classic RAM failure symptoms. Windows Memory Diagnostic (built-in) or MemTest86 (bootable, more thorough) are the correct tools to test RAM modules. SMART and CrystalDiskInfo test storage drives, not RAM.

practice_questions.q: Which PSU output voltage supplies power to fans, motors, and high-power components such as graphics cards?
options: 5V
practice_questions.explanation: The PSU delivers 12V for fans, motors, and high-power components (GPUs, optical drives). 5V and 3.3V rails power logic circuits and storage devices. Understanding which rail powers which component helps diagnose power delivery failures.

practice_questions.q: UEFI Secure Boot is failing on a system where a Linux distribution is being installed. The bootloader is not being executed. What is the most likely reason?
options: The Linux distribution uses GPT instead of MBR
The Linux bootloader is unsigned and not trusted by Secure Boot
Secure Boot only works with Windows
The CMOS battery is failing
practice_questions.explanation: Secure Boot validates the bootloader and OS kernel against cryptographic signatures before executing them. Some Linux distributions ship with unsigned or untrusted bootloaders. Installing such a distribution may require temporarily disabling Secure Boot, or the distribution must provide a signed bootloader recognized by the system's Secure Boot key store.

practice_questions.q: A technician notices that a RAID 5 array currently rebuilding after a drive replacement suddenly fails completely. What most likely caused the total array failure?
options: The new replacement drive was the wrong capacity
A second drive failed during the rebuild, exceeding RAID 5's fault tolerance
The RAID controller lost its configuration
The array was formatted as MBR instead of GPT
practice_questions.explanation: RAID 5 can tolerate only one drive failure. During a rebuild, the array is in a degraded state — if a second drive fails before the rebuild completes, the array loses all data. This is why the replacement drive must be installed and the rebuild completed as quickly as possible, and why removing the correct failed drive (not a good drive) before starting the rebuild is critical.

practice_questions.q: A laptop displays an image that is only visible when the screen is viewed at an extreme angle in bright light. What component has most likely failed?
options: The LCD screen panel itself (cracked internal glass)
The backlight (inverter or LED strip) — the image is visible but too dim due to backlight failure; the panel and GPU are functioning correctly
The GPU on the motherboard has partially failed and cannot output full brightness
The screen cable (LVDS/eDP) has a loose connection causing reduced voltage to the panel
practice_questions.explanation: When a laptop screen shows a very faint image visible only at an angle with bright external lighting, the LCD matrix and GPU are working — the backlight has failed. On older CCFL-backlit screens, the inverter board may have failed; on modern LED-backlit screens, the LED strip or backlight driver circuit is faulty.

practice_questions.q: After upgrading a PC's CPU with an aggressive overclock, the system experiences random crashes and blue screens under load. What is the FIRST corrective action?
options: Replace the CPU — it is incompatible with the motherboard
Revert the CPU to default clock speeds in BIOS/UEFI (disable overclocking or load optimized defaults) and test stability
Reinstall the operating system to clear corrupt overclock settings
Increase the page file size to compensate for memory errors caused by overclocking
practice_questions.explanation: Overclocking instability manifests as BSODs, random crashes, or failed stress tests. The first step is always to remove the overclock and restore factory defaults in BIOS. If stability returns at stock settings, the overclock was too aggressive — the voltages and frequencies must be tuned more conservatively.

practice_questions.q: A PC's USB keyboard and mouse work fine during POST but stop responding after Windows loads. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The USB ports shut down after POST as a BIOS power-saving feature
Missing or corrupted USB or HID (Human Interface Device) driver in Windows
The USB controller chip has failed and needs motherboard replacement
The keyboard and mouse are incompatible with Windows — use PS/2 adapters
practice_questions.explanation: USB devices functioning during BIOS/POST but failing in Windows indicate a driver issue rather than hardware failure. Windows loads USB and HID drivers to manage devices after boot — if these are corrupted or missing, input devices stop working. Booting to safe mode or using Device Manager to reinstall drivers resolves this.

practice_questions.q: A workstation produces no audio output. The audio driver is installed and Device Manager shows no errors. What should be checked next?
options: Replace the sound card immediately — Device Manager errors are not always shown for audio failures
Check Windows Volume Mixer for muted apps, verify the correct output device is selected in Sound Settings, and confirm physical speaker/headphone cable connections
Reinstall Windows — audio issues without Device Manager errors require a clean OS install
Update the BIOS — audio driver conflicts with UEFI are common on modern systems
practice_questions.explanation: No audio with no Device Manager errors is often a configuration issue, not hardware failure. Common causes include muted volume in the mixer, wrong output device selected (e.g., HDMI output selected instead of speakers), or disconnected cables. Always exhaust software and connection checks before replacing hardware.

practice_questions.q: After removing a PCIe expansion card, a PC boots but the monitor shows no image. The monitor works fine on another PC. What is MOST likely wrong?
options: Removing the expansion card shorted the PCIe slot and damaged the motherboard
The monitor cable may still be connected to the removed card's port, or the system is outputting video to the motherboard's integrated GPU port — switch the cable to the correct output
PCIe slots cannot be used after a card is removed — the slot must be disabled in BIOS
The CPU requires the expansion card to function and cannot boot without it
practice_questions.explanation: When a discrete GPU is removed, the system may switch video output to the motherboard's integrated graphics port. If the monitor cable is still plugged into where the discrete card was (now empty), there is no signal. Connecting the cable to the motherboard's video output resolves this immediately.
